<parameter name="content"># User Data Export: Implementation Tasks

Approved plan: build an API endpoint that exports all of a user's data. Use whatever format is easiest. Should be fast. Ship next week.

Items marked **[Decide]** are small decisions the plan leaves open. Make the call quickly, note it in the PR, and move on.

## 1. Scope and decisions (day 1, keep short)
- [ ] **[Decide]** Inventory the tables/services that hold user data and list what "all of a user's data" includes (profile, content, activity, settings, uploaded files). Record any intentional exclusions (e.g. internal flags, other users' data, password hashes/secrets).
- [ ] **[Decide]** Pick the export format. Default: JSON (easiest, native to most stacks). Use one top-level object with a section per data type, plus a `version` and `exported_at` field.
- [ ] **[Decide]** Pick the delivery model. Default: synchronous response if small, otherwise async job plus download link (see section 4).
- [ ] **[Decide]** Define "fast": a target such as p95 under N seconds for a typical user, and a size cap that triggers the async path.

## 2. API endpoint
- [ ] Add the route, e.g. `POST /api/users/me/export` (or `GET`, per the existing API conventions).
- [ ] Require authentication; a user may export only their own data. Admin or on-behalf-of access only if already supported elsewhere.
- [ ] Add rate limiting (e.g. a few exports per user per hour), since exports are expensive.
- [ ] Return appropriate status codes and headers (`Content-Type`, `Content-Disposition: attachment`) and error responses consistent with the rest of the API.
- [ ] Document the endpoint in the API docs/OpenAPI spec.

## 3. Data collection
- [ ] Write one collector function per data source, each returning a serializable structure for a given user ID.
- [ ] Build an export service that calls the collectors and assembles the final document.
- [ ] Stream or paginate large collections instead of loading everything into memory.
- [ ] Avoid N+1 queries: batch or join, and add indexes on `user_id` columns where missing.
- [ ] Run independent collectors concurrently where the stack allows it.
- [ ] Handle partial failures explicitly: fail the export clearly rather than silently returning incomplete data.

## 4. Large exports (only if the size cap from section 1 is exceeded)
- [ ] Enqueue a background job that generates the file and stores it in temporary storage.
- [ ] Add a status/download endpoint returning a short-lived, user-scoped signed URL.
- [ ] Notify the user when the export is ready (in-app or email, whichever already exists).
- [ ] Add expiry and cleanup of generated files.

## 5. Security and privacy
- [ ] Exclude secrets and credentials (password hashes, tokens, API keys, MFA seeds).
- [ ] Ensure no other user's personal data leaks through shared records (comments, messages, shared docs).
- [ ] Log export requests (who, when, outcome) for audit, without logging the exported content.
- [ ] Review authorization with a test that user A cannot export user B's data.

## 6. Testing
- [ ] Unit tests for each collector and for document assembly.
- [ ] Integration test for the endpoint: auth required, happy path, empty user, user with large data.
- [ ] Authorization and rate-limit tests.
- [ ] Basic performance test against a large seeded account to verify the "fast" target.
- [ ] Verify the output parses and contains every data source from the inventory.

## 7. Release
- [ ] Put the endpoint behind a feature flag.
- [ ] Add metrics and alerts: request count, duration, failures, output size.
- [ ] Deploy to staging and run a manual export with a realistic account.
- [ ] Roll out gradually, then enable for all users.
- [ ] Short internal note or runbook: what is included, the format, and how to troubleshoot failures.

## Suggested order
1. Section 1 (decisions) → 2. Sections 2 and 3 in parallel → 5 → 6 → 4 (if needed) → 7.
Critical path for next week's ship: sections 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7. Section 4 can follow if typical exports fit within the synchronous size cap.
</parameter>

jI wrote the breakdown to `tasks.md`. I used only your request text and didn't read or search anything else.

The plan leaves a few things open: what "all of a user's data" covers, the format, what "fast" means, and how large exports are handled. I didn't push back on the plan. I made them short **[Decide]** tasks at the top of the list, with defaults (JSON, synchronous response with an async fallback) so they don't block you.

I also added a security and privacy section (own-data-only access, excluding secrets, audit logging). Those items cost little now and are hard to retrofit after launch.

If you need to ship next week, the critical path is sections 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7. The async path in section 4 can follow if typical exports fit in a synchronous response.
